title: The quality pyramid
subtitle: Regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru
objectives: Read Grand Cru and Premier Cru labels
Explain the size of each level

steps.title: Four levels
steps.body: Burgundy's appellations form a pyramid. At the base, regional wines like Bourgogne, about half the production. Then village wines, named after a commune, like Gevrey-Chambertin. Then Premier Cru, named vineyards within a village, about 10%. At the top, 33 Grand Crus, about 1% of production.
steps.highlight: Regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru

steps.title: Reading the label
steps.body: A village wine names the village. A Premier Cru adds the vineyard, like Gevrey-Chambertin Premier Cru Clos Saint-Jacques. A Grand Cru names only the vineyard, like Chambertin or Montrachet. Many villages added their most famous Grand Cru to their name, so Gevrey became Gevrey-Chambertin. That can confuse: the village wine isn't the Grand Cru.
steps.highlight: Grand Crus name only the vineyard

steps.prompt: Order Burgundy's levels from broadest to most precise.
steps.explanation: Each level is smaller and more specific.

steps.title: Domaines and négociants
steps.body: Because vineyards are split among many owners, a single climat can appear on many labels. Domaines grow and bottle their own grapes; négociants buy grapes or wine and bottle under their own name. Producer matters as much as appellation in Burgundy.
steps.highlight: Producer matters as much as place

steps.prompt: About how many Grand Crus does Burgundy have?

steps.title: What you learned
points: Burgundy's pyramid: regional, village, Premier Cru, Grand Cru
Grand Crus name only the vineyard
Domaines and négociants both bottle; producer matters
